title: AI and Chip Leadership Peaks at Record Highs Before a Sharp Rout Tips Semis Into a Bear Market
content: The AI and semiconductor complex remained the market's engine through most of the window, driving the Dow above 53,000 and lifting the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to fresh records around mid-July, aided by SK Hynix's blockbuster Nasdaq debut and renewed enthusiasm for AI infrastructure spending. Leadership then cracked hard: the PHLX Semiconductor Index shed roughly 11% in the final week and fell almost 24% from its late-June peak, technically a bear market. Nvidia, AMD and Applied Materials led declines, while the rout spread across Asia, with SoftBank, Tokyo Electron and Advantest each down around 9%. Catalysts included underwhelming TSMC guidance, a new Chinese AI model and mounting scepticism over the scale of AI capex. With chip volatility at its highest since 2020 and index concentration extreme, the reversal dominated global equity sentiment and left breadth and positioning central to the tape.

title: Cooler CPI and an Oil Retreat Flip the Fed Narrative From Rate-Hike Risk to Hold
content: A hawkish Fed backdrop dominated early in the window, with markets assigning roughly 40% odds to a July hike as officials fretted over sticky prices. That narrative reversed sharply after the June CPI, released mid-July, undershot expectations: headline fell 0.4% on the month to 3.5% y/y, while core was flat and eased to 2.6% y/y. A 5.7% drop in energy, as US-Iran tensions de-escalated and Brent slid back from spikes near $78, did much of the work. July hike odds collapsed towards 10%, USTs rallied and yields fell across the curve, the two-year leading declines towards 4.1%. A firmer USD and higher real-rate expectations had earlier pressured gold, but the dovish repricing eased that strain. Markets still price around one hike by year-end, leaving each data print pivotal for rates, FX and rate-sensitive equities.

title: Japan's Bond Shock: JGB Yields Hit Multi-Decade Highs as the Yen Stays Weak
content: Japan re-emerged as a global macro flashpoint as the sell-off in government bonds accelerated through the window. The 10-year JGB yield reached 2.90% in early July, its highest since 1996, while the 20-year pushed towards 3.9%, as BoJ balance-sheet normalisation, firm inflation and fiscal anxiety over Prime Minister Takaichi's spending plans compounded. The move fed a broader repricing of the world's long end, reinforcing upward pressure on global term premia alongside the Fed debate. Yet the yen stayed conspicuously weak: despite a record 11.7trn yen of intervention deployed in the spring, USD/JPY drifted back above levels authorities had defended, with rising domestic yields failing to arrest the slide. The combination revived carry-trade and intervention chatter and kept Japanese duration, long dismissed as inert, firmly back in investors' cross-asset toolkit, a slow-burn risk with global spillover potential.
